title: The UK has passed 3,000 padel courts. Bubble? Not even close.
text:
The Court Report · October 2026

The UK has passed 3,000 courts.
Bubble?

Not even close, but some towns are already full

James Morgenstern · 25 October 2026 · 10 minute read

The UK now has 3,061 padel courts open across 891 clubs. That is the count on Padel Genie's live map as of 25 October 2026, covering England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

It's a huge milestone for the sport. Especially since most people in Britain had never heard of 'Padel' a few years ago. But a national total only tells you part of the story, and certainly doesn't answer the question of whether there's a bubble (or not).

The real story is where the courts are, where they are not, and what is coming next. Here's what the data shows:

The pipeline is deep. At least 1,266 courts were approved in the last 12 months, and at least 1,082 more are awaiting a decision.
Councils are saying yes. They approved 85% of the new padel schemes they decided in the last year.
The map is lopsided. Hertsmere has 26 courts per 100,000 people. 38 councils with more than 100,000 residents have none inside their boundary. If you're interested, Padel Genie can show you exactly where these are.
London is underserved. At 3.8 courts per 100,000 people, it is the lowest of any English region.
Northern Ireland is the surprise. At 6.5 courts per 100,000 people, it is level with the North West as the best-served part of the UK.
Scotland and Wales lag behind. Scotland has 112 courts across 40 clubs, just 2.1 per 100,000 people and less than half the GB average. Wales has 110 courts across 30 clubs, about 3.5 per 100,000.

Every open padel club in the UK on Padel Genie's live map, grouped by region. Screenshot from 25 October 2026.

Today's numbers

England holds almost nine in ten UK courts, but every nation now has more than 100.

Nation | Courts open | Clubs open | Courts per 100,000 people |
England | 2,715 | 795 | 4.8 |
Northern Ireland | 124 | 26 | 6.5 |
Scotland | 112 | 40 | 2.1 |
Wales | 110 | 30 | 3.5 |
UK | 3,061 | 891 | 4.6 |

Clubs are still small. The average UK club has 3.4 courts, and the median is 3. The largest is Carbon Padel Club in Manchester with 17 courts. Rocket Padel Bristol and Padel Bonito in Sheffield follow with 14 each.

The UK is building indoors. Nearly half of UK courts (48%) are fully indoor, 16% are covered with open sides, and 35% are outdoor. Outdoor can still make good money, but the share of indoor and covered courts is rising fast.

The pipeline: what's coming next

Behind the 3,061 open courts, at least 2,348 more courts are either approved or awaiting a planning decision.

Well over 100 new padel applications, approvals and openings land across the UK every month, and any one of them can change a catchment's opportunity score overnight. Not every approval will get built. But even so, the direction is clear.

Our modelling shows there will be at least 4,000 courts open by this time next year. Supply isn't slowing down anytime soon.

Stage | Schemes or clubs | Courts |
Announced and coming soon | 47 clubs | 226 |
Approved in the last 12 months | 569 new schemes | at least 1,266 |
Awaiting a planning decision | 449 new schemes | at least 1,082 |

Approved and awaiting figures are floors.

Planning is not the bottleneck. Councils approved 85% of the new padel schemes they decided in the last 12 months: 569 approvals against 99 refusals. A further 67 were withdrawn. Count those as not approved and the rate is still 77.4%.

Decisions take about three and a half months. The median new scheme took 105 days from validation to decision. The middle half took between 64 and 164 days. Extensions of time are routinely agreed, so plan for it rather than fight it.

Where councils approved the most. East Riding of Yorkshire approved 12 new schemes in the last year and Sheffield 10. South Downs National Park, Sefton and Bromley approved 7 each. Sheffield stands out: it already has 51 open courts, the third most of any council.

The lopsided map

Across Great Britain there are 4.5 courts for every 100,000 people, but that average hides huge swings from one town to the next. If there is one absolute truth about padel it is this:

Saturation is local, not national.
A national total tells you nothing about whether your town can take another club. The only question that matters is how saturated your catchment is.

By region. The North West leads Great Britain with 6.5 courts per 100,000 people. London has just 3.8, the lowest of any English region, despite the hype around padel in the capital. Scotland has 2.1, less than half the GB average.

North vs South. UK padel started in London and the South East, but per head the North West now leads every region in Great Britain. Four of the five councils with the most open courts are in the North: Cheshire East (57), North Yorkshire (53), Sheffield (51) and Leeds (45), with Birmingham (48) the other.

The next wave is northern too. East Riding of Yorkshire, Sheffield and Sefton are among the councils approving the most new schemes, and as our August Court Report found, many of the biggest are conversions of empty industrial units.

The South hasn't stalled; it has spread outwards. The most saturated councils sit in London's commuter belt, like Hertsmere, Welwyn Hatfield and Mid Sussex, while London itself is the most underserved English region.

Northern Ireland punches well above its weight. It has 124 courts for about 1.9 million people, or 6.5 per 100,000. That puts it level with the North West as the best-served part of the UK, and three times Scotland. Much of that is one operator: Let's Go Padel runs 13 of its 26 clubs.

By council, the gap is even wider. The most saturated councils have three to six times the GB average.

And at the other end. 38 councils with more than 100,000 residents have no open padel court inside their boundary. That is the natural place to start looking for your next site, and it is exactly what Padel Genie is built for.

Understanding saturation. Everyone in padel has a number in their head for where the UK tops out. Spread evenly across the population, 5,000 courts would be about 7.5 per 100,000 people, and 10,000 would be about 15. Today it's 4.6. Whatever your number, the job is the same: find the catchments still below it. In Padel Genie you set your own saturation level with a slider, and it shows you every catchment that still has room.

Who is building UK padel

No single operator dominates. The largest network holds about 6% of UK courts, and every other operator holds under 3%.

No single model is winning yet. Groups like David Lloyd and Powerleague are adding a few courts to sites they already run, a smart, low-risk way in. Dedicated operators like Let's Go Padel, PadelHub and Pure Padel are building bigger clubs from scratch, averaging five to six courts each. Others pair padel with gyms, studios or food and drink, and the mix varies by region. We'll dig into what's working where in a future post, so sign up to the newsletter if you haven't already.

Bubble or not?

If you've read it this far, you're deeply invested in padel and probably also saw Bloomberg's article questioning if the 'bubble was about to burst'. In our opinion, that's nonsense. Not only was their data out of date, but there is no national bubble, only local ones.

The question is never "is UK padel saturated?" It is "is this catchment saturated?"

Peak demand is strong. Across 593 clubs we track occupancy and court revenue for, courts were 70% booked at peak times and 31% off-peak between 24th September and 23rd October 2026.

Club X-Ray: occupancy, price and estimated revenue for every bookable club. Club names are blurred here, not in the product. Screenshot from 24 October 2026.

That gap is the real story. As everyone knows, evenings and weekends are busy almost everywhere. Daytime weekday slots are where clubs make or lose their margins, and that depends on the people living around the club: who they are, when they're free and how far they'll travel.

A word of warning. Occupancy data is fascinating, but it only tells you how the past went. It says nothing about where a catchment will be in 12 or 24 months, once the pipeline opens. As they say in investing, past performance is no guide to the future.

Demographics is destiny. Two catchments a few miles apart can be completely different markets. In one, the daytime courts fill with sessions and coaching for the over-65s. In the next, younger players pack out the evenings, and tournaments and food and drink do the heavy lifting. Household income shapes the rest: whether premium pricing holds, and whether a Pilates studio or a café earns its space.

The best sites are chosen with all of that in mind. Padel Genie's demographics show you who lives in any catchment, and exactly where your target market lives within it.

Croydon's demographics in Padel Genie: padel fit, age profile and income, mapped area by area.

Location decides the outcome. If you're entering an already highly saturated market, it's always going to be an uphill battle. No amount of marketing can fix a bad location decision and pricing will always come under pressure. But for operators finding great sites on good leases, the market is roaring, and talk of a bubble misses the point.

What it means for you

Operators. Planning approval is likely; the site decision is the risk. Before committing to a lease, look at the courts already open within a realistic drive, everything approved or pending in the same catchment, and the population behind it. Then run numbers at different saturation points, model the headroom and assess the demographics. A town with no open club can still be a bad bet if three approved schemes sit ten minutes away and the catchment is too small.

Investors and landlords. Ask any operator pitching a site for its catchment numbers, including the pipeline, not just today's competition. The 1,082 courts awaiting a decision today will change a lot of catchments over the next 18 months. Padel Genie puts that whole pipeline on the map, catchment by catchment, so you can see tomorrow's market today.

Suppliers and builders. Your next customers are in the planning system right now. 569 schemes were approved in the last year and 449 more are waiting. Every one of them needs courts, canopies, lighting, tech, financing and security. The applicant on each one is a lead long before the club opens.

How we count

Courts open are courts physically at a club that is taking bookings, including singles courts and members-only clubs. The count covers England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and moves daily as clubs open.
Planning figures count new schemes only, leaving out condition discharges, variations and other paperwork on schemes already approved.
Courts in planning are a floor. Where an application says "courts" without a number we can determine (for example a warehouse change of use), we count two, the minimum. This means the true number is higher.
Council figures count courts inside each council's boundary, so a club named after a town can sit just outside it.
Occupancy comes from the booking systems of 593 clubs, as a simple average across clubs. Blocked-out courts count as booked.
Population figures are from the 2021 Census (ONS and NISRA).

All figures are as of 25 October 2026 unless stated.
